lessons.title: Downstream and Upstream Speeds
lessons.concept: In boats and streams, the speed of water current affects effective speed. Downstream means moving with the current, so effective speed increases. Upstream means moving against the current, so effective speed decreases. Let boat speed in still water be b and stream speed be s.
lessons.formula: Downstream speed = b + s. Upstream speed = b - s (assuming b > s).
lessons.worked_example: Boat speed in still water 10 km/h, stream 2 km/h. Downstream = 12 km/h, upstream = 8 km/h.
mistakes: Assuming stream speed can be greater than boat speed for upstream travel (impossible to move upstream in that case)
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Finding Boat and Stream Speeds
lessons.concept: If downstream speed (D) and upstream speed (U) are known, we can find boat speed in still water and stream speed by solving the two equations: b+s=D, b-s=U.
lessons.worked_example: Downstream 15 km/h, upstream 9 km/h. Boat speed = (15+9)/2 = 12 km/h. Stream speed = (15-9)/2 = 3 km/h.
mistakes: Swapping formulas for b and s

lessons.title: Time, Distance, and Round Trips
lessons.concept: Use time = distance/speed with effective downstream/upstream speeds. For round trips (same distance downstream and upstream), total time is sum of times for each leg. Average speed for equal distances is not the simple average of speeds.
lessons.formula: Time downstream = d/(b+s). Time upstream = d/(b-s). Total = d/(b+s) + d/(b-s).
lessons.worked_example: Distance 24 km, b=10, s=2. Downstream time = 24/12=2 h. Upstream time = 24/8=3 h. Total = 5 h.
mistakes: Using still-water speed for travel time in current
Taking simple average of speeds for round trip time
Unit mismatch between distance and speed

options.B: An impossible situation given same boat/stream
